Preface

When asked about my profession, I often find it hard to provide a simple answer. My career has led

me through various paths and roles over time. As someone deeply passionate about learning and

exploring new things, I’ve had the opportunity to work in numerous fields.

I’ve worked in software development, advertising, marketing, network and telecom, systems

administration, training, technical writing, computer repair, and other fields. I’ve always been driven

by the desire to learn more and expand my horizons. As I learned new technologies, met new people,

and explored new concepts, my mind became more open and my perspective widened. I began to

see connections and possibilities that I had never seen before.

The more I learned, the more I desired to teach, even for free sometimes. I cherish the moment when

someone finally gets a concept they’ve been struggling with. Being a teacher at heart, I’ve always

enjoyed sharing my knowledge.

This is precisely what inspired me to write this guide.

While writing this guide, I constantly considered its future readers. My aim was to create an

accessible, easy-to-follow guide on NLP, GPT, and related topics for Python developers with limited

knowledge in these areas. My goal was to provide practical information that readers could use to

build their own intelligent systems without needing to spend years learning the theory behind

these concepts.

In this practical, hands-on guide, I share my knowledge and experience with OpenAI’s AI models,

specifically GPT-3 and GPT-4, as well as other models. I explain how Python developers can use

them to add intelligence to their new or existing applications.

This guide is designed as a step-by-step manual that covers the fundamental concepts and techniques

of using AI/ML and OpenAI models, providing a hands-on approach to learning.

My inbox is always full, as I receive numerous emails. However, the most rewarding ones are from

readers who have found my online guides and courses useful. Please feel free to reach out to me at

aymen@faun.dev¹ and share your testimonial - I would love to hear from you.

I hope you enjoy reading this guide as much as I enjoyed writing it.

in various roles, responsibilities, and projects in the technology field, including DevOps & Cloud

The Story of OpenAI and ChatGPT

In December 2015, a group of brilliant minds united with a shared goal: to foster and develop friendly

AI for the benefit of all humanity.

Sam Altman⁷, Elon Musk⁸, Greg Brockman⁹, Reid Hoffman¹⁰, Jessica Livingston¹¹, Peter Thiel¹²,

Amazon Web Services (AWS), Infosys, and YC Research announced the establishment of OpenAI,

pledging over US$1 billion to the initiative. The organization declared its intention to “freely

collaborate” with other institutions and researchers by making its patents and research publicly

available.

OpenAI’s headquarters are located in the Pioneer Building in San Francisco’s Mission District. In

April 2016, OpenAI launched a public beta of “OpenAI Gym”, a platform for reinforcement learning

research. In December 2016, OpenAI unveiled “Universe¹³”, a software platform designed to measure

and train an AI’s general intelligence across a wide array of games, websites, and other applications.

In 2018, Elon Musk stepped down from his board seat, citing “a potential future conflict of interest”

with Tesla’s AI development for self-driving cars, but continued to support the organization as a

donor. In 2019, OpenAI transitioned from a non-profit to a capped-profit entity, with a profit cap

set at 100 times any investment. The company distributed equity to its employees and formed a

partnership with Microsoft, which announced an investment of US$1 billion in the company. OpenAI

subsequently announced plans to commercially license its technologies.

In 2020, OpenAI unveiled GPT-3, a language model trained on trillions of words from the internet.

They also announced that an associated API, simply named “the API”, would form the basis of

its first commercial product. GPT-3 is designed to answer questions in natural language, but it

can also translate between languages and generate coherent improvised text. In 2021, OpenAI

introduced DALL-E, a deep-learning model capable of generating digital images from natural

language descriptions.

Fast forward to December 2022, OpenAI received widespread media coverage after launching a free

preview of ChatGPT. According to OpenAI, the preview attracted over a million signups within

the first five days. Anonymous sources cited by Reuters in December 2022 projected OpenAI’s

revenue at US$200 million for 2023 and US$1 billion for 2024. As of January 2023, the company

was in discussions for funding that would value it at $29 billion.

This is the brief history of OpenAI, an artificial intelligence research laboratory composed of the

for-profit OpenAI LP and its parent company, the non-profit OpenAI Inc.

The Story of OpenAI and ChatGPT 4

Most people were unaware of OpenAI until the company released its popular ChatGPT.

The primary purpose of ChatGPT was to mimic human behavior and engage in natural conversations

with people. However, the chatbot can learn and teach itself based on the conversations it has with

different users. This AI has conversational capabilities and can write tutorials and code, compose

music, and perform other tasks. The use cases for ChatGPT are quite diverse and potentially limitless,

as users have demonstrated. Some use cases are creative (e.g., writing a rap song), others are

malicious (e.g., generating malicious code or commands), and still, others are business-oriented (e.g.,

SEO, content marketing, email marketing, cold emails, and business productivity).

ChatGPT, standing for Generative Pre-trained Transformer, is built on top of OpenAI’s GPT family

of large language models (LLMs). The chatbot is fine-tuned using both supervised and reinforcement

learning techniques.

GPT-3 served as the foundation for ChatGPT before the release of GPT-3.5 on March 15, 2022,

followed by GPT-4 on March 14, 2023. ChatGPT is a project that utilizes GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, and

adds a web interface, memory, and more user-friendly features. After reading this guide, you will

be capable of building your own chatbot, potentially better than ChatGPT, since you can customize

it to your specific needs.

You may have seen the chart comparing the two versions of GPT, showing the number of parameters

in GPT-3 (175 billion) and GPT-4 (100 trillion).

How Does GPT Work?

The Generative Pre-trained Transformer, or GPT, is a generative text model. This model can produce

new text by predicting what comes next based on the input it receives.

GPT-4 is another model that is larger and more performant than any previous GPT model, including

GPT-1/2/3/3.5.

The 4th generation was trained on a large corpus of text, such as books, articles, and publicly

accessible websites like Reddit and other forums. It uses this training data to learn patterns and

relationships between words and phrases.

GPT-4’s key innovation lies in its impressive size - boasting billions of parameters - making it one of

the most massive and powerful language models ever devised. Its extensive training on such a vast

dataset enables it to generate human-like text, execute various natural language processing tasks,

and complete tasks with impressive accuracy.

GPT is a type of neural network known as a transformer, which is specifically designed for natural

language processing tasks. The architecture of a transformer is based on a series of self-attention

mechanisms that allow the model to process input text in parallel and weigh the importance of each

word or token based on its context.

Self-attention is a mechanism used in deep learning models for natural language processing (NLP). It

allows a model to weigh the importance of different parts of a sentence or multiple sentences when

making predictions. As part of the Transformer architecture, it enables a neural network to achieve

satisfactory performance in NLP tasks. The concept of self-attention is based on the idea that each

word in a sentence can be influenced by other words in the sentence, and the importance of each

word can be determined based on its context. The original work on self-attention was introduced in

the paper “Attention is All You Need²⁰”.

To better illustrate the concept of self-attention, consider the following analogy:

Imagine attending a large dinner party where everyone is sharing stories simultaneously. You’re

trying to follow all the conversations around you, but naturally, you focus more on the stories that

are relevant to you or contain important information. As people speak, you give your attention to

the storyteller whose narrative is currently most interesting or relevant, sometimes switching focus

based on new information or connections you make to other stories being told.

In this analogy, you are like the transformer model in GPT. The dinner party represents the input

text, where each guest’s story is a word or token in the sequence. Your ability to listen to multiple

stories at once and decide which one to focus on is similar to the self-attention mechanism. This

mechanism allows the model to process all parts of the input simultaneously and determine the

²⁰https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762

relevance or importance of each word in the context of all the others, much like you tuning into the

most engaging story at any given moment.

Let’s see a quick code example. This is an example of using Hugging Face Transformers for GPT-2

inference:

1 from transformers import pipeline

2 generator = pipeline(

3 'text-generation',

4 model = 'gpt2'

5 )

6 generator(

7 "Hello, I'm a language model",

8 max_length = 30,

9 num_return_sequences=3

10 )

This is an example of an output from the code above:

1 [

2 {

3 'generated_text':

4 "Hello, I'm a language model. So while writing this, ..."

5 },

6 {

7 'generated_text':

8 "Hello, I'm a language model. I write and maintain ..."

9 }

10 ]

By default, a model has no memory, this means that each input is processed independently, without

any information being carried over from previous inputs. When GPT generates text, it doesn’t

have any preconceived notions about what should come next based on previous inputs. Instead,

it generates each word based on the probability of it being the next likely word given the previous

input. This results in text that can be surprising and creative.

This is another example of code that uses a GPT model to generate text based on user input.

20 print("AI: " + generated_text)

GPT-4 was designed as a general-purpose large multimodal model, which means that it can be

used for a wide variety of natural language processing tasks (such as language translation, text

summarization, and question answering) and multimodal tasks (such as text-to-image generation

and image captioning). OpenAI has trained GPT-4, but you can base your own model on your fine-

tuned datasets. This enables more creative and specific use cases, in addition to the default tasks the

model can assist with, such as generating text, poetry, and stories. It can also be used for building

chatbots that are experts in a specific domain, other conversational interfaces, and more!

In this guide, we will dive deep into OpenAI models (GPT, embeddings, and more) and how to use

them in Python, including how to effectively utilize the API and the tools provided by the company

and the AI/ML community to prototype powerful and creative tools and systems. This will not only

enhance your proficiency in using the GPT API but also broaden your understanding of the concepts

and techniques used in natural language processing, AI/ML and other related fields.

GPT is considered a significant advancement in natural language processing because of its extensive

scale. However, some experts have voiced concerns about the possibility of the model creating

prejudiced or damaging content. As with any technology, it’s super important to take a step back

and consider the ethical implications of its use. This guide will not cover the ethical issues but will

only focus on the practical technical aspects.

Happy coding!

Development Environment Setup

Notes

This guide frequently uses the “heredoc” syntax for file creation and content insertion directly from

the command line or within scripts and programs.

ℹ Heredoc, an abbreviation for “here document,” is a shell scripting feature that facilitates

the creation of multiline strings.

The heredoc syntax starts with << followed by a delimiter token of your choice, continues with the

content you want to include, and concludes with the same delimiter token on a new line. This syntax

is especially beneficial for scripting and programming tasks that require file generation or multiple

lines of input for a command.

To use the heredoc syntax for file creation or content appending, use the following structure:

1 cat << EOF > filename

2 This is line #1

3 This is line #2

4 ..

5 EOF

In this example, <<EOF signifies the start of the heredoc section, and EOF on a separate line indicates

its end. The content between these markers is redirected into “filename”. Replace “filename” with

the file name you prefer and modify the content as necessary.

The primary purpose of using heredoc syntax in this guide is to enable readers to create files

accurately and effortlessly with a single copy-paste action. This approach ensures that the author’s

exact content is replicated in the reader’s environment, reducing the likelihood of manual errors and

making the learning experience more effective.

I suggest copying and pasting the heredoc examples directly into your terminal to create the files

and content as intended.

Windows users can execute the heredoc examples using the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL).

Alternatively, you can manually create the files and paste the content using a text editor. However,

I recommend using a Unix-like environment (preferably a Debian-based system) to follow the

examples in this guide.

text:
Development Environment Setup 12

If you’re using a different system, you may need to adjust some minor details, such as the package

manager, the installation process for packages, and the method for creating files and directories.

This shouldn’t pose a problem, as the examples are straightforward and can be easily adapted to any

system.

Another important note worth mentioning is that this guide is structured in a way where each

chapter builds upon the previous one, with topics and concepts interwoven throughout to form

a comprehensive understanding of the subject matter. It’s important for you to progress through

the chapters sequentially, taking the time to fully grasp each section before moving on to the next.

Patience and attention to detail will greatly enhance your learning experience, allowing you to fully

benefit from the structured progression.

The code presented in this guide is not meant to be passively read but actively executed. Engaging

with the code - running it, modifying it, and observing the outcomes—is important for a deep

understanding of the concepts discussed. This hands-on approach will help you internalize the

material and develop the skills necessary to apply the concepts in your own projects.

Installing Python, pip, and a Virtual Development

Environment

First and foremost, you’ll need Python. For the purposes of this guide, we’ll be using Python 3.9.5.

We’ll also be using pip, which is a package installer for Python. Pip allows you to install packages

from the Python Package Index and other indexes.

Don’t worry if you don’t have Python 3.9.5 installed on your system. We’re going to create a

virtual development environment, so regardless of the version you currently have, your development

environment will be isolated from your system and will use Python 3.9.5.

If Python isn’t already installed on your system, head over to www.python.org/downloads/²¹,

download, and install one of the Python 3.x versions. The instructions you’ll need to follow will

vary depending on your operating system.

To manage our development environment, we’ll be using virtualenvwrapper²². You can find the

installation instructions in the official documentation²³.

1 pip install --upgrade pip

2 pip install virtualenv

3 pip install virtualenvwrapper

For Windows users, you can use the following command to install virtualenvwrapper-win²⁴:

²³https://virtualenvwrapper.readthedocs.io/en/latest/install.html

²⁴https://github.com/davidmarble/virtualenvwrapper-win/

If pip isn’t installed, the simplest way to install it is by using the “get-pip.py²⁵” script:

Development Environment Setup 14

Obtain Your OpenAI API Keys

The subsequent step involves generating API keys that will grant you access to the official API

provided by OpenAI.

Visit platform.openai.com²⁶ to create an account, then generate your API keys²⁷.

An API key can be associated with an organization, and you’ll be prompted to create one. In this

guide, we’ll name it: “LearningGPT”.

Ensure to store the generated secret key in a safe and accessible location. You won’t be able to retrieve

it again through your OpenAI account.

Install the Official Python Bindings

While you can interact with the API using HTTP requests from any language, this can be done either

via the official Python bindings, the official Node.js library, or a community-maintained library.

In this guide, we’ll utilize the official library provided by OpenAI. Another option is Chronology²⁸, an

unofficial library offered by OthersideAI. However, this library appears to be no longer maintained,

and its use in production is not recommended.

To install the official Python bindings, execute the following command:

1 pip install openai==1.9.0

Ensure that you’re installing the library in the virtual environment we created earlier.

Test our API Keys

Firstly, let’s set the API key and the organization ID as environment variables:

1 export API_KEY=xxx

2 export ORG_ID=xxx

Now, you can run the following command to test the API:

The models Babbage-002 and Davinci-002 are both part of the GPT-3 series developed by OpenAI,

and they serve as replacements or upgrades to previous models:

• Babbage-002: Serves as a replacement for the GPT-3 Ada and Babbage base models. It’s

optimized for tasks that require a balance between performance and cost-efficiency and is

suitable for moderately complex tasks like text classification, semantic search, and basic

language understanding.

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text: Understanding the Available Models and Which One to Use 20 • Davinci-002: Replaces the GPT-3 Curie and Davinci base models. It’s known for its advanced language understanding and generation capabilities and is ideal for more complex tasks that require nuanced understanding, such as content creation, complex language translation, and solving sophisticated problems. • DALL-E 3 and DALL-E 2: Both are image generation models. DALL-E 3 is an improvement over DALL-E 2 - a basic model, with more advanced capabilities in generating high-resolution, realistic images from text descriptions. • Whisper-1: This model is specialized in speech recognition and transcription. It was designed to convert spoken language into written text accurately. In the future, you may see more advanced versions of this model (e.g., Whisper-2, Whisper-3, etc.). • GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-3.5-Turbo-Instruct: All of these models are variants of GPT-3.5 designed for more efficient and responsive text generation. • GPT-4: This is a large multimodal model that can accept both text and image inputs. It is the successor to GPT-3 and is capable of performing a wide range of tasks. Some of the models listed in the output are dynamic, as they are subject to continuous updates by OpenAI. For example, GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, and GPT-4-32k point to the latest model version. At the time of writing, the latest GPT-4 model is GPT-4-0613, so when your code calls the GPT-4 API endpoint, you are actually using GPT-4-0613. In the future, when OpenAI releases a new GPT-4 model, the API endpoint will point to the new model. This is why it is recommended to use a specific version of the model in your code if you have specific requirements. Historically, models used to be called “engines”, but OpenAI deprecated the term “engine” in favor of “model”. Some resources use these terms interchangeably, but the correct name is “model”. When using the API, requests that use the old names will still work, as OpenAI has ensured backward compatibility, but this could change in the future. However, some models should be manually replaced by newer ones. It is recommended that you use the updated models to avoid any issues in the future. Some models are not listed above, like the moderation models. These models are used to detect inappropriate content in text and to filter it out. The usage of these models is optional but highly recommended if you are building a public application. You don’t want your users to receive inappropriate results. Which Model to Use? There is no single answer to this question. It depends on your use case and the type of application you are building. In general, you should use the most recent model available. For example, from a functionality perspective, if you are building a chatbot, you should use the GPT-3.5-Turbo-Instruct model. If you are building an application that generates images from text, you should use the DALL- E 3 model. If your application requires more capabilities, you should use the GPT-4 model. The second factor to consider is pricing. Some models

If your application requires more capabilities, you should use the GPT-4 model. The second factor to consider is pricing. Some models are more expensive than others. For example, GPT-3.5-Turbo is the most cost-effective model in the GPT-3.5 series.

text:
Understanding the Available Models and Which One to Use 21

Another important factor is the context window. Some models have a larger context window than

others. For example, the GPT-4-32k model has a context window of 32,768 tokens (about 50 pages

of text) while the GPT-4-0613 model has a context window of 8,192 tokens (about 12 pages of text).

This means that the GPT-4-32k model can process more text than the GPT-4-0613 model.

In the following sections, we are going to take a closer look at the main models that are available;

this will help you understand the differences between them and choose the right model for your

application. However, it is important to understand that some of the models listed below are

deprecated and probably won’t be available in the future. OpenAI is constantly improving its models

and deprecating old ones.

OpenAI Model Series

GPT-4 Series

GPT-4 is the latest model series developed by OpenAI and is the successor to GPT-3. One of the main

differences from GPT-3 is that GPT-4 models are multimodal. This means that GPT-4 can accept both

image and text inputs.

ℹ In general, multimodal deep learning is a subfield of deep learning that enriches models

with information collected from various data modalities, such as text, images, video, audio,

and sensor data. This puts it a step ahead of traditional machine learning, which was

confined to a single modality, thus addressing the complexity surrounding real-world data

that often blends various sources. The objective is to create a unified representation space,

capturing diverse information from these modalities useful in tasks like image captioning,

speech understanding, and natural language processing.

GPT-4 demonstrates human-level performance on several professional and academic benchmarks.

Notably, GPT-4 achieved a score in the top 10% on a simulated bar exam, a significant improvement

from GPT-3.5, which scored in the bottom 10% according to a blog post²⁹ published by OpenAI.

GPT-4 is available for developers using the API and regular users using ChatGPT.

There are two main models in the GPT-4 family:

• Standard GPT-4 (8k) model with a context length of 8,192 tokens.

• Extended GPT-4 (32k) model with a context length of 32,768 tokens (about 50 pages of text).

However, other models are available for specific use cases like GPT-4-Turbo, a model that accepts

images as input in the Chat Completion API.

The InstructGPT-3 is superior to the base GPT-3 in following instructions. It presents four distinct

Base GPT-3 Series

The foundational GPT-3 series comprises four models (A, B, C, D), each varying in speed and

performance.

• Ada (A): Suitable for basic tasks, typically the quickest and most cost-effective in the GPT-3

lineup.

• Babbage (B): Handles elementary tasks with speed and at a reduced cost.

• Curie (C): Highly efficient, offering faster performance at a cost lower than Davinci.

• Davinci (D): The pinnacle of GPT-3 models, excelling in quality across tasks the other models

undertake.

The base GPT-3 models are capable of understanding and generating human language and text

that appears to be natural language. They are also capable of performing a large number of tasks,

including:

• Text classification

• Semantic search

• Text summarization

• Sentiment analysis

• Content generation

• Text completion

• Text translation

• Text extraction

However, this series is not the most accurate in the GPT-3 series.

The embedding model is a model that can be used to embed text into a vector space. This operation

Using GPT Chat Completions

OpenAI models were trained as completion-style models, which means they are designed to predict

the next word in a sequence of text. This is a common task in natural language processing, and it’s

also the basis for many other tasks such as translation, question answering, text analysis, and more.

To use the chat completions, you need to have an OpenAI API key. You can generate this in your

OpenAI dashboard³⁶. Then, you need to use the API endpoint to send a request to the API and get

a response back.

OpenAI provides multiple models. However, if you’re starting out, choose between GPT-3.5-Turbo

or GPT-4.

An Introductory Example

Let’s initiate a chat with GPT-3.5:

The response is a ChatCompletion object. This object contains the following keys:

• id: This is the ID of the completion. You can use this ID to retrieve the completion later.

• created: This is the timestamp of when the completion was created.

• model: This is the model that was used to generate the completion.

• object: This is the type of the object. In this case, it’s a chat completion.

• system_fingerprint: A parameter used to identify the backend configuration of an OpenAI

model, helping to track if changes in this configuration affect the output determinism.

• usage: This is an object that contains the number of tokens used in the prompt, the number of

tokens generated by the model, and the total number of tokens (prompt + generated).

• Finally, the response contains a list of choices. Each choice contains the following keys:

- finish_reason: This is the reason why the completion stopped. It can be stop, length,

function_call, content_filter or null. stop means that the completion stopped because it

reached a stop sequence. length means that the completion stopped because it reached the

maximum token count. function_call means that the completion stopped because it reached

a function call. content_filter means that the content was flagged by the content filter. null

means that the API still has more tokens to generate.

- index: This is the index of the choice in the list of choices.

- logprobs: This is a list of log probabilities for each token in the completion. This is useful if

you want to know the probability of each token in the completion.

- message: This is the message that was generated by the model. It contains the following keys:

- content: This is the content of the message.

- role: This is the role of the message. It can be user or assistant.

- function_call: This is the function call that was used to generate the message. This is useful

if you want to know how the message was generated.

- tool_calls: This is a list of tool calls that were used to generate the message. This is useful if

you want to know how the message was generated.

If you want to obtain the content of the message, you can use the following code:

1 print(response.choices[0].message.content)

System, User and Assistant Roles

When we sent the request to the API, we used the messages parameter. This parameter is a list of

dictionaries. Each dictionary contains the role and the content of the message. There are three

possible roles:

• system: This is the initial prompt used to set the context and behavior of the assistant.

• user: This role represents the user and is used to send a message to the model.

• assistant: This role represents the assistant (the AI model) and is used to send a message to

the user.

The System Role

The messages list should contain at least one message with the system role. This is an example:

The content of the message with the system role was used above to define the behavior of the

assistant. In this case, the model is designed to respond to the user in an intelligent and creative

manner. It can also establish the context of the conversation. For instance, if you want to discuss

movies, you can set the context by using the following message:

1 {

3 "content": "You are a movie expert."

4 }

The User Role

The messages list can contain one or more messages with the user role. This is an example:

The content of the message with the user role is used to define the instructions for the model. In

The Assistant Role

The use of the assistant role is optional but can be useful in some cases. For example, if you want

to train the model to respond to the user in a specific way, you can use the assistant role to show

the model how to respond. Some examples are shown later in this guide.

Few-shot Learning with Chat Completions

Few-shot learning is a technique that allows you to train a model on a small dataset to perform a

specific task. This is useful when you don’t need to or can’t train it on a large dataset.

response.choices[0].message.content)). This is the output:

1 1. The Great Pyramid of Giza

We guide the model using a completion approach. “Completion” is like filling in the blanks. By

providing a starting point (our prefix), we tell the model how we want our output to start. The

model then completes or fills in the rest based on our instruction.

In other words, this is like providing the first half of a sentence and asking someone to finish it. The

model takes our starter (prefix) and provides a suitable continuation. This powerful feature allows

us to get specific outputs from the model without providing every detail; the model fills in the gaps

based on its training.

Our code could be improved by adding a stop sequence to the API call. The goal is to stop the

completion when the model reaches the end of the list, instead of adding the note at the end. We

will understand how to do this in the next sections.

Controlling the Output’s Token Count

The length of the output is determined by the API. Let’s see an example:

1 CompletionUsage(

2 completion_tokens=107,

The completion_tokens represent the number of tokens generated by the model. The prompt_tokens

represent the number of tokens used in the prompt. The total_tokens is the sum of completion_-

tokens and prompt_tokens.

ℹ Tokens, by definition, are common sequences of characters in the output text. A good

way to remember this is that one token usually equates to about 4 letters of text for

standard English words. This means that 100 tokens are approximately equivalent to 75

words.

To control the length of the output, you can use the max_tokens parameter. This parameter is a

number that depends on the model. For example, the max_tokens for the GPT-3.5-Turbo model is

4095. Here is an example showing two different outputs with different max_tokens values:

33 print("Long response:")

34 print(long_response.choices[0].message.content)

35 EOF

When we define max_tokens=50 or max_tokens=300, we are instructing the API to halt the completion

once it reaches 50 or 300 tokens. The token count is calculated by the API, incorporating both the

tokens in the prompt and those generated by the model. If the prompt contains more tokens, the

API will generate fewer tokens in the completion. This is why selecting the appropriate max_tokens

value is crucial for user experience.

ℹ Consider max_tokens as a budget for a shopping trip. The tokens you start with in

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text:
Using GPT Chat Completions 46

the prompt are like items already in your cart before you begin shopping (initial cost).

The money you have represents the total amount you can spend. So, if your cart already

contains some items (the longer prompt), you have less space for new items (the model-

generated text) (fewer tokens left). If you start with an almost empty cart (the shorter

prompt), you will have more space for subsequent items. Thus, the max_tokens setting

is akin to managing a budget to ensure you acquire everything you need within an

affordable amount.

OpenAI API pricing is not only based on the number of tokens returned in the completion_tokens

but also on the number of total_tokens. This means that the prompt_tokens are also counted in the

pricing.

Controlling When the Completion Output Stops

If you execute the previous code, there’s a high chance that the short response will be cut off. Here’s

an example:

1 Short response:

2 Hannibal, also known as Hannibal Barca, was a Carthaginian general who lived in anci\

3 ent times. He is best known for his leadership during the Second Punic War, where he\

4 famously fought against Rome. Hannibal is famous

Even with a higher token count, the response may still be cut off. To avoid this, you can use the stop

parameter. This parameter is a list of strings that typically contains one or more of the following

stop sequences:

• ”.”: This is the period character. It tells the API to stop the completion when it reaches a period.

This means that the completion cannot continue after providing the first sentence.

• “\n”: This is the newline character. It tells the API to stop the completion when it reaches a new

line.

• “user:”: This is the user role. It tells the API to stop the completion when it reaches the generated

text from the user. This means that the completion cannot change the role from the assistant

to the user.

• “assistant:”: This is the assistant role. It tells the API to stop the completion when it reaches

the assistant role. Like the previous one, it means that the completion cannot switch to the

assistant role.

Let’s start with this example that prints a very short response:

14 "Who is Hannibal?"

15 },

19 response = client.chat.completions.create(

20 model=model,

21 messages=messages,

22 max_tokens=50,

23 stop=[stop_token],

26 print(response.choices[0].message.content + stop_token)

The stop tokens are defined in the stop parameter as a list. In this case, we are using the period

character as the stop token. That’s why the API replies with a single sentence.

Temperature and Hallucination

Imagine if a model were a human, complete with creativity and imagination. Sometimes, they might

be overly excited and creative, while other times they might be too conservative and lack creativity.

It all hinges on the context and situation.

In the world of generative models, this is referred to as “temperature”. A high temperature makes

the model more creative and likely to generate new words. Conversely, a low temperature makes

the model more conservative, favoring words it has seen before.

However, there are instances where the model might be too “hot”, generating words unrelated to

the context. This is known as “hallucination”. Hallucination is a common issue in generative models,

and a significant challenge for researchers is finding ways to mitigate it.

Practically, in the case of OpenAI GPT models, the temperature parameter determines the wildness

or conservatism of the model’s outputs. A higher temperature, close to 2.0, makes the model’s

responses more random and creative, sometimes even “hallucinating” information that may not

be strictly accurate. Conversely, a lower temperature, like 0.2, makes the model more focused,

conservative, and deterministic, adhering closely to the data it was trained on. A temperature of

1.0 is a good middle ground for most use cases.

The temperature parameter is a number between 0.0 and 2.0, with the default value being 1.0.

Sampling with Top_p

top_p can be an alternative to temperature for controlling the randomness of text generation in

models like GPT-3 or GPT-4. Both parameters influence how the model generates text, but they do

so in different ways.

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development

Using GPT Chat Completions 55

ℹ Think of top_p as if you were in an ice cream shop with a variety of flavors. You intend

to mix up some flavors, but you’re not sure which ones to pick. However, you’d like to

stick to the ones most likely to be pleasant for you. In this scenario, top_p is like telling

the server, “Please give me a scoop of the most popular flavors, but only until we reach a

certain level of popularity.” The server then scoops out the most popular flavors, one by

one, until the total popularity of all the scoops in your cone reaches the level you specified.

More technically, while generating text, each AI model actually leaves several next words, or tokens,

as possibilities. Each of these tokens, in fact, has some probability of being a correct continuation

of the current sequence of words. top_p sampling means the model will only consider the most

probable next words that, added together, reach a certain cumulative probability (the top_p value).

For example, using 0.5 means only the tokens with the highest probability mass, comprising 50%,

are considered. Using 0.1 means the tokens with the highest probability mass, comprising 10%, are

considered.

The top_p parameter is a number between 0.0 and 1.0. The default value is 1.0.

One Should I Use?

removed from the set of candidates. This means that the model will be less likely to generate new

words.

As you can see, the output is almost the same. This is because a low temperature and a low top_p

both reduce the creativity of the model. However, since they work in different ways, the output may

be slightly different.

You should choose to use the temperature when you want to control the overall creativity and

randomness of the model. For example, if you want the same predictable output for the same input,

you should use a low temperature value. Very high temperature values could lead the generated

text to meander off-topic by introducing new ideas that are not related to the context.

You should choose to use the top_p when you want to control the randomness of the model while

keeping the output deterministic. For example, if you want to control the diversity of the output

while keeping identical inputs deterministic, you should use a low top_p value.

ℹ Using both temperature and top_p is possible but not recommended. Both parameters

aim to control the randomness and diversity of the model output, but they do so in

ways that can overlap or conflict with each other. If you decide to experiment with both,

proceed with caution and conduct extensive testing to understand their interaction in

your specific use case.

Controlling Repetitivity: Frequency and Presence

Penalties

The OpenAI API provides two parameters to adjust the generation of text, ensuring both diversity

and uniqueness:

1. The presence_penalty defines how much the model penalizes repeated use of the same topic

or terms within a response. A higher presence penalty encourages the model to introduce new

concepts and terms, leading to more varied and diverse outputs. It’s particularly useful when

you want the model to explore new ideas and avoid redundancy.

2. The frequency_penalty defines how much the model penalizes the repeated use of the same

word or phrase. This penalty encourages the model to use a wider vocabulary and prevents it

from repeating itself excessively in the generated text. A higher frequency penalty makes the

model less likely to reiterate words or phrases it has already used, resulting in more diverse

and therefore more original output.

Both values are numbers between 0.0 and 2.0, with the default value being 0.0.

the difference between the outputs:

Frequency vs. Presence Penalty

There are some key differences between the frequency_penalty and presence_penalty parameters.

If you’re wondering which one to use, experiment with both to understand their effects on the

model’s outputs. However, it is important to understand the fundamental difference between the

two.

ℹ Imagine you’re a DJ at a party and your main job is to choose and play songs that keep

the party going. You have two controls in your DJ booth:

• Frequency Penalty (Repetition Control): Think of this as the “Repeat Song” button.

If you set it to a high value, it means you don’t want to play the same song again

anytime soon. If you set it to a low value or negative, you’re okay with playing the

same song or its variants more often.

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text:
Using GPT Chat Completions 62

• Presence Penalty (Diversity Control): This is like the “Genre Shuffle” knob. If you

use this, you’re telling the system you want to hear a wider variety of music genres.

A high value means you’re adventurous and want to include songs from genres you

haven’t played yet. A low value or negative means you’re sticking to the current

genres and not expanding much into uncharted territories.

Now, imagine you’re DJing at a party where people love 80’s hits. If you set both controls

high, you’ll play a broad variety of 80’s songs and never repeat the same track. But if you

reduce the “Repetition Control” (Frequency Penalty), you might play the favorite hits like

“Billie Jean” or “Sweet Child O’ Mine” more frequently, while still exploring a wide variety

of other 80’s hits due to the “Genre Shuffle” (Presence Penalty) being high.

These two controls allow you to adjust between keeping the crowd’s favorites on loop

versus introducing them to new hits they might love. Similarly, in the context of the

OpenAI GPT models, these parameters determine how often it uses familiar tokens versus

exploring new and diverse ways of “expressing” itself.

Advanced Examples and Prompt

Engineering

What is Prompt Engineering?

Prompt engineering is a new area within artificial intelligence, focused on creating and refining

instructions for language models like GPT models. Good prompts can improve the model’s output

in terms of quality and relevance.

This discipline requires understanding the model and analyzing its training data to spot any biases.

By tweaking the instructions and model parameters, prompt engineers can make AI behavior more

accurately align with user needs, resulting in more dependable results.

OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, called prompt engineering an “extremely impactful skill and an early

form of programming in a bit of natural language” in a tweet.

Prompt Engineering according to Sam Altman

Prompt engineering is a key field that’s gained attention with the rise of AI language models like

GPT-3. Its importance lies in directing these models with specific instructions, or prompts.

Language models learn from large amounts of text data, but generating coherent, relevant responses

can be hard. They may give irrelevant or biased answers, particularly when prompts are vague or

poorly formed.

Prompt engineering started with early language model development. To make models more useful

and user-friendly, it became clear that the generated text needed explicit instructions. Early prompts

were simple, but often resulted in generic or poor responses.

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text:
Advanced Examples and Prompt Engineering 66

Key models like GPT-4, LaMDA, Llama 2, and PaLM marked the start of this field. They learned

from a lot of text data to generate coherent, contextually correct responses. For instance, GPT-4 is

thought to have an impressive 170 trillion parameters, while Llama’s largest model has 65 billion

parameters, and PaLM, Google’s 540 billion parameter transformer model, powers its AI chatbot,

Bard, brilliantly. But, even these models needed clear instructions to give the right outputs, leading

to the growth of prompt engineering.

The importance of this field grew with the launch of text-to-image models like Stable Diffusion,

Midjourney, and DALL-E, which generate images from text prompts but need specific instructions

to give the right outputs.

Prompt engineering has borrowed from fields like NLP, computational linguistics, and human-

computer interaction. Various strategies to design prompts that give precise, contextually correct

responses have been studied.

text:
Advanced Examples and Prompt Engineering 68

Prompt engineering presents several challenges due to the absence of a standardized approach. This

lack of clear guidelines complicates comparisons across various models and applications.

Addressing these challenges involves a variety of mature prompt engineering techniques. We’ll

examine some of these techniques in the following section, focusing on their potential to enhance

performance.

Few Shot Learning: A Key Prompt Engineering

Technique

In this example, we aim to extract keywords from a text and return a list of these keywords. We

have two potential approaches to solve this problem:

• We can instruct the model to generate a list of keywords.

• We can provide the model with examples of texts and keywords, and ask it to generate

keywords for a new text.

We will utilize the second approach because typically providing examples to the model results in

better performance and allows us more control over the output without needing to write additional

text for user prompt explanations. We will also use the temperature parameter to limit the model’s

creativity, as this type of task requires a certain level of determinism.

ℹ Adapting the temperature parameter to the task is a crucial step in achieving the best

results. For instance, if we are generating a tweet, we can use a high value for the

temperature parameter because we want the model to be creative. However, if we are

generating a list of keywords, we can use a low value for the temperature parameter

because we want the model to be deterministic.

Overgeneration and Selection

In this example, we will use GPT-4 for social media posts. The text below will be our starting point

for the tweet:

1 The first programming language to be invented was Plankalkül, which was designed by \

2 Konrad Zuse in the 1940s, but not publicly known until 1972 (and not implemented unt\

3 il 1998). The first widely known and successful high-level programming language was \

4 Fortran, developed from 1954 to 1957 by a team of IBM researchers led by John Backus\

5 . The success of FORTRAN led to the formation of a committee of scientists to develo\

6 p a "universal" computer language; the result of their effort was ALGOL 58. Separate\

7 ly, John McCarthy of MIT developed Lisp, the first language with origins in academia\

8 to be successful. With the success of these initial efforts, programming languages \

9 became an active topic of research in the 1960s and beyond.

The issue is that this text is too lengthy for a tweet (731 characters). We also need to incorporate

hashtags into the tweet, limiting the final tweet to a maximum of 280 characters.

We will select the most crucial keywords from the previous example for the hashtags. Hence, we

will execute two API calls:

• The first API call will generate the keywords.

• The second API call will create the tweet.

When the output of one prompt is the input of another, it’s termed “prompt chaining”. More

specifically, it’s “sequential prompt chaining” as the output of the first prompt is the input of the

second.

The challenge lies in crafting a tweet within the 280 character limit. A common issue with LLMs

like GPT-4 is their tendency to disregard user-defined limits in the prompt. To address this, we’ll

employ three techniques:

1. We’ll use the few-shot learning technique, providing the model with examples of tweets that

adhere to the 280 character limit. This will help the model learn to create tweets within this

limit.

2. We’ll use the temperature parameter to constrain the model’s creativity, thereby reducing the

risk of generating an overly long tweet. This task doesn’t necessitate high creativity. A certain

level of determinism might suffice for a good tweet. Suitable temperature values could range

from 0.5 to 1. Experimenting with different values to find what works best is also recommended.

3. We’ll generate multiple tweets and select the one that fits within the 280 character limit.

In this example, we are going to see how to generate a rap song with a certain subgenre, for example,

old-school rap. To get better results, we are going to use a technique called General Knowledge

Prompting³⁸ which consists of generating knowledge about the task by the model and then use this

knowledge to feed the model and generate the output.

In this example, context stuffing is used to guide the model to generate specific configuration scripts.

The model is given examples of what is expected (a Dockerfile for Node.js, a Kubernetes deployment

for Redis) and then asked to generate similar content for a different technology (Python Dockerfile,

Let’s imagine a software company that wants to automate their technical support process. The

company provides a variety of products, including cloud services, developer tools, and enterprise

solutions. The company’s customer support often deals with technical queries that require specific

and detailed responses. To enhance efficiency and accuracy, the company implements a chatbot

using context stuffing techniques to handle complex technical queries. This is how it works:

• The chatbot first categorizes incoming queries based on keywords, product names, and the

nature of the query (e.g., troubleshooting, configuration, best practices).

• Based on the result of the categorization process, the chatbot prepares a contextually relevant

prompt. For example, if a query is about configuring a cloud service, the chatbot will preload

examples of similar configurations.

• The chatbot uses these context-stuffed prompts to generate specific, relevant answers. This

may include step-by-step guides, code snippets, or troubleshooting advice.

• If the initial response is not sufficient, the chatbot uses follow-up questions from the user to

further refine the context and provide more accurate answers.

This approach improves the technical support quality.

• The defined prompt requires 17 tokens.

max_tokens parameter as follows:

What’s Next?

The effectiveness of the Chat Completions API’s results is fundamentally influenced by the

parameters we employ. However, this is not the only determinant of the quality of operate. In

fact, the quality of the prompt, the set of examples used, the methodology applied in coding and

problem-solving, and the clever thinking of the user all play a significant role in shaping the quality

of results.

For this reason, it is of utmost importance to invest time in conceptualizing the problem at hand

and determining the most effective strategy to address it. This requires a deep understanding of the

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text:
Advanced Examples and Prompt Engineering 110

problem, a thoughtful approach, and an innovative mindset. Moreover, careful consideration should

be given to the construction of the prompt and the selection of examples.

One effective strategy for this is to imagine the problem and its solution being explained to a human.

This can help ensure that the prompt and examples are clear, concise, and practical. Additionally,

providing the model with examples of the desired output can be beneficial. This can guide the model

and help it understand what is expected of it.

Furthermore, experimentation plays an important role in getting better results. It is important and

necessary to experiment with various parameters, methodologies, prompts, and examples, and to

iterate on them based on feedback and outcomes. This iterative process can lead to continuous

improvement and ultimately, the best possible results.

In addition, employing the correct prompt engineering technique is critical for achieving optimal

results. The choice of the right technique, based on the use case, can greatly influence the

effectiveness of the model. In reality, prompting cannot be called “an exact science,” as it requires

a lot of trial and error to achieve the best results. However, there are some best practices, rules of

thumb, proven methods and occasionally tricks and hacks that can help improve results depending

on the use case and the LLM you are using.

Few-shot learning, zero-shot learning, and general knowledge prompting are not the only prominent

prompt engineering techniques. Others include Chain of Thought (CoT), Zero-shot CoT, Auto Chain

of Thought (AutoCoT), Self-consistency, Transfer Learning, ReAct (Reason + Act), and more. Each

technique has its own strengths and weaknesses.

If you are interested in this field, my guide, “LLM Prompt Engineering For Developers: The Art and

Science of Unlocking LLMs⁴⁰’ True Potential”, provides in-depth explanations of these techniques.

Embedding

What is an Embedding?

If we were to describe this feature in one sentence, we would say that text embedding represent text

strings as vectors in high-dimensional space, enabling the measurement of similarity between them.

Embeddings, in general, are commonly used for tasks such as finding the most relevant results for

a search query, grouping text strings based on their similarity, recommending items with similar

text, identifying text strings that greatly differ from others, analyzing the differences between text

strings, and labeling text strings based on their closest match.

From a practical standpoint, embeddings represent real-world objects and relationships in the form

of vectors (lists of numbers). This same vector space measures the similarity between two entities.

Use Cases: From Modern Search Engines to Self-Driving

Cars

OpenAI’s text embedding measure the relatedness of text strings and can be used for a variety of

purposes.

These are some use cases:

• Natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as sentiment analysis, semantic similarity, and

sentiment classification.

• Generating text-embedded features for machine learning models, such as keyword matching,

document classification, and topic modeling.

• Generating language-independent representations of text, allowing for cross-language compar-

ison of text strings.

• Improving the accuracy of text-based search engines and natural language understanding

systems.

• Creating personalized recommendations by comparing a user’s text input with a wide range

of text strings.

We can summarize the use cases as follows:

• Search: where results are ranked by relevance to a query string

• Clustering: where text strings are grouped by similarity

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text:
Embedding 112

• Recommendations: where items with related text strings are recommended

• Anomaly detection: where outliers with little relatedness are identified

• Diversity measurement: where similarity distributions are analyzed

• Classification: where text strings are classified by their most similar label

Following are some practical approaches to using embeddings (not necessarily using the OpenAI

platform).

Tesla: How Embeddings Are Used in Self-Driving Cars

Working with unstructured data, such as raw text, pictures, and videos, can pose challenges. It’s

often difficult to obtain original data due to privacy issues, and building models from scratch can

require significant computational power, vast datasets, and ample time.

Embedding offer a solution by enabling the transfer of information from one context (like an image

of a car) to another (such as a game). This process, known as transfer learning, allows us to train

models without the need for extensive real-world data.

Companies like Tesla leverage this technique for their self-driving cars.

Kalendar AI: The Power of Embedding in Sales Outreach

Kalendar AI is a sales outreach tool that uses embedding to match the appropriate sales pitch to the

right customers, drawing from a dataset of 340 million profiles.

This automation is based on the similarity between embeddings of customer profiles and sales

pitches, ranking the most suitable matches. According to OpenAI, this method has reduced

unwanted targeting by 40–56% compared to their previous approach.

Notion: Enhanced Search Capabilities

Notion, an online workspace tool, has enhanced its search capabilities by leveraging OpenAI’s em-

beddings. This advancement goes beyond the basic keyword-matching systems the tool previously

employed.

With this new feature, Notion can more adeptly understand the structure, context, and significance

of the content stored on its platform. This enables users to execute more accurate searches and

retrieve documents more efficiently.

DALL·E 2: Text-to-Image Conversion

DALL·E 2 is a system designed to convert text labels into images.

It operates using two models named Prior and Decoder. The Prior model processes text labels to

generate CLIP⁴¹ image embeddings. Subsequently, the Decoder takes these CLIP image embeddings

and crafts a learned image. This image is then upscaled from a resolution of 64x64 to 1024x1024.

⁴¹https://openai.com/blog/clip/

The Python program we wrote prints a list of floating-point numbers such as 0.010284645482897758

or 0.013211660087108612. These floating points represent the embedding of the input text “I am a

programmer” generated by the OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 model.

The embedding is a high-dimensional representation of the input text that captures its meaning. This

is sometimes referred to as a vector representation or simply an embedding vector.

An embedding is fundamentally a method of representing an object, like text, with an array of values.

Each value signifies a distinct facet of the object’s meaning, reflecting the intensity of that facet for

that particular object. For text, these facets might encompass topics, sentiments, or other semantic

characteristics.

In simpler terms, the vector representation generated by the embedding endpoint translates data into

a format comprehensible by machine learning models and algorithms. It’s a method to transform a

specific input into a form readily usable by these models and algorithms.

ℹ When using the embeddings model text-embedding-ada-002, it is important to note

that the input (in our case, “I am a programmer”) must not exceed 8191 tokens in length.

This limit could be different for other embeddings models. Given that 100 tokens roughly

equate to 75 English words, the maximum input for the text-embedding-ada-002 model is

approximately 6,143 words (8191 tokens x 0.75). With an average English page containing

about 500 words, this translates to around 12.29 pages of text.

We are going to explore how to use embeddings in the following sections.

text: Embedding 116 Use case: Semantic Search Forget about OpenAI for a moment and let’s get back to the world of search engines, which is the best way to understand what semantic search is - everybody uses search engines! Search engines were created to help us find the information we need. However, the way we search has changed over time. In the past, we used to search for keywords and search engines were like an old-school index card system. They would match the keywords in the search query with the keywords in the index and return the results. It used to be a simple lexical search. You’d get a list of links that contain the keywords you searched for. Now, we search for concepts and ideas. We ask questions and expect answers. We want to find the information we need, not just a list of links. How the tables have turned! Welcome to the world of semantic search. Imagine going to a bookstore, and instead of looking for a book yourself, you just mention a vague idea about what you’re in the mood for. “A book about a young wizard in a magical school,” you’d say. And instantly, the bookstore owner, who seemingly has an uncanny ability to read minds - or at least, to understand you better than you understand yourself - nods knowingly and, with a smile, hands you a “Harry Potter” book. That is the magic of semantic search on the web. With conventional keyword-based searches, search engines function somewhat like old-fashioned librarians. You provide them with a term, and they retrieve a list of documents where that term is present. It’s all very literal and often doesn’t quite hit the mark. But semantic search? It’s like a perceptive bookstore owner. It strives to understand you. It values context, synonyms, and even your individual history and preferences. It’s not solely about what you typed, but rather what you intended - because, indeed, humans are complex in that way. How does this magic work? Mainly, by harnessing vector search. Words are transformed into high- dimensional vectors, positioning them in a space where ‘conceptual proximity’ matters more than exact wording. Add a dash of machine learning to this mix, and the system refines itself over time. It learns from countless queries, your search history, and context to become eerily adept at serving up what you actually want, not just what you say you want. In the following section, we are going to understand how to implement this vector search using OpenAI’s text embeddings. Cosine Similarity: A Deeper Look In the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), cosine similarity is a commonly used metric to measure the similarity between documents, regardless of their size. From a mathematical perspective, it calculates the cosine of the angle between two vectors projected in a multi-dimensional space. It examines the angle between two vectors and compares them. The result is a number between -1 and 1. If the vectors are identical, the result is 1.

It examines the angle between two vectors and compares them. The result is a number between -1 and 1. If the vectors are identical, the result is 1. If the vectors are completely different, the result is -1. If the vectors are at a 90-degree angle, the result is 0.

text:
Embedding 117

ℹ Imagine two hikers starting from the same point in a forest and walking outwards in

different directions. If they both walk straight ahead without turning, they’re following

very similar paths. In the context of cosine similarity, we’d say their paths (or vectors)

are almost identical, with a cosine similarity close to 1. Now, imagine one hiker decides

to take a left turn, and the other turns right. Their paths are now diverging, just like two

vectors pointing in different directions. If they walk in completely opposite directions,

their paths (vectors) are entirely dissimilar, giving a cosine similarity close to -1. So, the

smaller the angle between their paths, the more similar their journeys are. Similarly, in

NLP, the smaller the angle between two vectors (or the closer the cosine value is to 1), the

more similar the two documents are.

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text:
Embedding 118

The analogy of hikers in the forest

The formula for cosine similarity is:

$$

Similarity = (A.B) / (||A||.||B||)

$$

• A and B are vectors.

• “A.B” is a method of multiplying two sets of numbers together. This is done by multiplying

each number in one set with the corresponding number in the other set, then summing all of

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text:
Embedding 119

those products.

• ||A|| is the length of vector A. It’s calculated by taking the square root of the sum of the squares

of each element in vector A.

Consider vector A = [2,3,5,2,6,7,9,2,3,4] and vector B = [3,6,3,1,0,9,2,3,4,5].

Here’s how we can calculate the cosine similarity between them using Python:

1 cat > src/app.py << EOF

2 import numpy as np

3 from numpy.linalg import norm

4

5 # define two vectors

6 A = np.array([2,3,5,2,6,7,9,2,3,4])

7 B = np.array([3,6,3,1,0,9,2,3,4,5])

8

9 # print the vectors

10 print("Vector A: {}".format(A))

11 print("Vector B: {}".format(B))

12

13 # calculate the cosine similarity

14 cosine = np.dot(A,B)/(norm(A)*norm(B))

15

16 # print the cosine similarity

17 print(

18 "Cosine Similarity between A and B: "

19 f"{cosine}"

20 )

21 EOF

The next step involves using cosine similarity to find the word most similar to a user-specified search

term. Here’s how we’ll do it:

We’ll start by reading the new file and converting the last column into a NumPy array, as this is

necessary for calculating cosine similarity. Our embedding, when saved to a CSV file, are written as

strings. However, to use these embedding for any mathematical computation, such as finding cosine

similarity, we need them in a structured and efficient format - a NumPy array.

ℹ Essentially, NumPy arrays are widely used in numerical calculations. A regular data

structure like a list doesn’t provide much help with this kind of calculation. In addition to

that, an array consumes less memory and is faster. This is due to the fact that an array is

a collection of homogeneous data-types that are stored in contiguous memory locations,

Behind the Scenes: How Embeddings Work

The concept of embeddings is not new. It has been around for a long time. However, it has gained

popularity in recent years due to the rise of deep learning and the success of word embeddings like

Word2Vec, GloVe, and FastText.

The ability of embeddings to understand that “Apple” is nearer to “Banana” compared to “Dog” is a

result of how embeddings capture semantic relationships between words based on their usage and

context in large datasets. This process can be broken down into a few key components:

• Training on context: Embeddings are generated by training models on massive text corpora.

These models, such as Word2Vec⁴³, GloVe⁴⁴, or BERT⁴⁵, learn by observing how words are used

in sentences. For instance, “Apple” and “Banana” might frequently appear in similar contexts

related to fruit, food, eating habits, or nutrition, whereas “Dog” appears in contexts related to

animals, pets, or outdoor activities.

⁴³https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word2vec

⁴⁴https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GloVe

⁴⁵https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BERT_(language_model)

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text:
Embedding 138

• Capturing semantic relationships: Through training, the model learns to associate words with

their contexts. This means that words appearing in similar contexts are positioned closer

together in the embedding space. The model doesn’t understand the meaning of “Apple” or

“Banana” in the human sense but recognizes that these words share similar usage patterns,

distinguishing them from “Dog,” which has different associations.

• High-dimensional vector space: In the high-dimensional vector space, each word is represented

as a vector (a point in space). The distance between these points is a measure of semantic

similarity. Techniques like cosine similarity are used to measure how close or far apart these

vectors are. “Apple” and “Banana” will have vectors that are closer together, while “Dog” will

be positioned further from these two.

Learning from co-occurrences: The underlying principle is that words with similar meanings will

co-occur in similar contexts more frequently than words with unrelated meanings. This principle,

often encapsulated in the saying “You shall know a word by the company it keeps⁴⁶,” allows the

embedding model to infer that “Apple” and “Banana” are related (both being fruits) and both are

quite distinct from “Dog.”

⁴⁶https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Rupert_Firth

The download_nltk_data function is designed to ensure that the necessary datasets and models

required by the NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit) library are available for use in your Python

environment. Here’s a breakdown of the datasets and models that we are downloading:

• ‘tokenizers/punkt’: This is for the Punkt tokenizer model, which is used to divide a text into a

list of sentences using an unsupervised algorithm.

• ‘corpora/stopwords’: This is a dataset of ‘stopwords’, which are words like ‘is’, ‘in’, ‘at’, ‘which’,

etc., that are usually removed in the preprocessing step in NLP tasks.

The preprocess_text function is designed to preprocess text by tokenizing, converting to lowercase,

removing punctuation, removing stopwords, and stemming. Here’s a breakdown of what each step

does:

• Tokenization: This is the process of splitting text into a list of words or sentences. In our case,

we are using the word tokenizer to split the text into a list of words.

• Converting to lowercase: This process converts all the words in the text to lowercase. This is

done to reduce the vocabulary size, as words like ‘The’ and ‘the’ are treated as different words

by the tokenizer.

• Removing punctuation: This process removes punctuation from the text. Punctuation is not

useful for our task, so we remove it.

• Removing stopwords: Stopwords are words like ‘is’, ‘in’, ‘at’, ‘which’, etc., that are usually

removed in the preprocessing step in NLP tasks. We remove them because they are not useful

for our task.

• Stemming: This process converts words to their root form. For example, ‘running’ is converted

to ‘run’. This is done to reduce the vocabulary size, as words like ‘running’ and ‘run’ are treated

as different words by the tokenizer.

Advanced Embedding Examples 144

Before proceeding, we will open a parenthesis to explain stemming and an alternative to it,

lemmatization. Both stemming and lemmatization are techniques used to reduce words to their

base or root form, but they approach this task differently:

Stemming simplifies words by cutting off the ends in a somewhat blunt manner, without considering

the context or meaning of the word. It’s a quick and dirty way to get to the root form, but it can

sometimes be inaccurate because it merely removes suffixes based on common patterns.

Lemmatization, on the other hand, is a more sophisticated process that considers the word’s meaning

and its grammatical role in a sentence. It uses a dictionary or a morphological analysis of words to

accurately reduce them to their base or dictionary form (lemma).

If you run the following code, you will see the difference between stemming and lemmatization:

1 import nltk

2 from nltk.stem import PorterStemmer

3 from nltk.stem import WordNetLemmatizer

4

5 # Download necessary NLTK data

6 nltk.download('wordnet')

7 nltk.download('omw-1.4')

8

9 # Initialize stemmer and lemmatizer

10 stemmer = PorterStemmer()

11 lemmatizer = WordNetLemmatizer()

12

13 # List of words to process

14 words = [

15 'running',

16 'runner',

17 'jumps',

18 'easily',

19 'better'

20 ]

21

22 # Stemming process

23 stemmed_words = [

24 stemmer.stem(word) for word in words

25 ]

26

27 # Lemmatization process with POS specification

28 # (POS: Part of Speech)

29 lemmatized_words = []

30 for word in words:

31 # Default to noun

38 pos_tag = 'v'

39 elif word in ['easily']:

40 # Treat this example as an adverb

41 pos_tag = 'r'

42 else:

43 # Treat all other examples as nouns

44 pos_tag = 'n'

45 lemmatized_word = lemmatizer.lemmatize(

46 word,

1 Original: ['running', 'runner', 'jumps', 'easily', 'better']

2 Stemmed: ['run', 'runner', 'jump', 'easili', 'better']

3 Lemmatized: ['run', 'runner', 'jump', 'easily', 'good']

Based on the output, we can see that stemming simplifies “running” to “run” because it identifies

and removes the “-ing” suffix according to its rule set. Stemming follows predefined rules without

understanding the context or the full morphological analysis of words.

Lemmatization, on the other hand, aims to correctly identify the base form of words (“lemma”)

by considering their meaning and part of speech (pos) within the context. So, “running” would be

lemmatized to “run” when identified as a verb, thanks to the lemmatizer’s understanding of word

forms and their grammatical roles. The same applies to “better” which would be lemmatized to

“good” when identified as an adjective while stemming would keep it as “better”.

ℹ Stemming is faster and simpler but less accurate than lemmatization. Lemmatization is

more accurate but slower and more complex than stemming.

input_coffee_index = df[df['name'] == input_coffee_name].index[0] uses Pandas’

For example, df[df['my_column'] == my_value] selects rows from the DataFrame df where the

value in the my_column column equals my_value.

This code returns a new DataFrame that only contains the rows meeting this condition. The resulting

DataFrame has the same columns as the original DataFrame df, but only the rows that meet the

condition.

For instance, if df is a DataFrame of coffee reviews (which is our case), and my_column is the

“name” column, then df[df['name'] == 'Ethiopia Yirgacheffe'] would return a new DataFrame

containing only the reviews for the “Ethiopia Yirgacheffe” coffee.

Next, we use index[0] to get the index of that row. index[0] retrieves the first index of the resulting

filtered DataFrame returned by df[df['name'] == input_coffee_name].

In other words, here is a breakdown of what each part of the code does:

“name” column equals input_coffee_name and False for all other rows.

2. df[df['name'] == input_coffee_name] uses this boolean mask to filter the DataFrame and

returns a new DataFrame containing only the rows where the “name” column equals input_-

coffee_name.

3. df[df['name'] == input_coffee_name].index returns the index labels of the resulting filtered

DataFrame.

4. index[0] retrieves the first index label from the resulting index labels. Since the filtered

DataFrame only contains one row, this is the index label for that row.

function from the openai.embeddings_utils module to calculate the cosine similarity between the

input coffee’s review and the current review. (We have used this function in a previous example.)

Next, let’s obtain the indices of the most similar reviews, excluding the input coffee’s review itself.

1 # Get the indices of the most similar reviews

2 # (excluding the input coffee's review itself)

3 most_similar_indices = \

4 np.argsort(similarities)[-6:-1]

If you have used NumPy before, you’re likely familiar with argsort, so you can skip the following

explanation. If it’s your first time, here’s a quick explanation:

np.argsort(similarities)[-6:-1] uses NumPy’s argsort() function to get the indices of the top

5 most similar reviews to the input coffee’s review. In other words, argsort() returns the indices

that would sort the similarities array in ascending order.

Consider this example: similarities = [0.8, 0.5, 0.9, 0.6, 0.7, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1, 0.0].

Here’s how np.argsort(similarities)[-6:-1] would work:

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text:
Advanced Embedding Examples 149

1. np.argsort(similarities) would return the sorted indices: [9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 1, 3,

0, 2]. The array is sorted based on the values of similarities: similarities[0] = 0.8,

similarities[1] = 0.5, similarities[2] = 0.9, etc.

2. np.argsort(similarities)[-6:-1] would return the 6th to the 2nd indices from the end of

the sorted array: [5, 4, 1, 3, 0].

When np.argsort(similarities) is called, it returns an array of indices that would sort the

similarities array in ascending order. In other words, the first index in the sorted array corresponds

to the element in similarities with the smallest value, while the last index corresponds to the

element with the largest value.

Consider the example [0.8, 0.5, 0.9, 0.6, 0.7, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1, 0.0]. The index of the

smallest value (0.0) is 9, the index of the second-smallest value (0.1) is 8, and so on. The resulting

sorted array of indices is [9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 1, 3, 0, 2].

This sorted array of indices is then used to get the indices of the top 5 most similar reviews by slicing

the array to get the 5th to 1st elements from the end of the array: [5, 4, 1, 3, 0]. These indices

correspond to the most similar reviews in descending order of similarity.

You may ask, why aren’t we using [-5:]?

If we used np.argsort(similarities)[-5:] instead of np.argsort(similarities)[-6:-1], we

would get the five most similar reviews, including the input coffee’s review itself. We exclude the

input coffee’s review from the most similar ones because it’s not helpful to recommend the same

coffee that the user has already tried. By using [-6:-1], we’re excluding the first element from the

slice, which corresponds to the input coffee’s review.

You might wonder why the review itself is in the similarity array.

The review was added to the review_embeddings array when we created embeddings for each review

using the get_embedding() function.

indices] returns the rows of the DataFrame that correspond to the 4th, 5th, 1st, and 3rd most similar

reviews.

Then, we use ['name'] to get the name column of those rows. Finally, we use tolist() to convert

the column to a list. This gives us a list of the names of the most similar coffees.

with Embeddings

This example introduces a zero-shot news classifier that predicts the category of a news article.

ℹ A zero-shot classifier refers to a classification model or system that can correctly

categorize data into classes that it has not seen during training. The term “zero-shot”

indicates that the model hasn’t been trained (i.e., seen zero examples) on those particular

classes, but it can still make predictions about them. This contrasts with the typical

supervised learning paradigm, where a model is trained on specific classes and can only

predict those classes.
