After executing the code above using python src/app.py, you should see the precision score. If the

precision score is 0.6, this means that the classifier was able to correctly predict the category of 60%

of the headlines in the dataset. If the precision score is 0.8, this means that the classifier was able to

correctly predict the category of 80% of the headlines in the dataset, and so on.

Understanding that precision has no fundamentally definitive meaning on its own is crucial. It is

relative to the source of truth used, which, in our case, is the “news.json” dataset. Using a different

dataset (or a different subset of the same dataset) will yield a different precision score.

Precision in Zero-Shot Classifier Applications:

Examples

Precision in a zero-shot classifier is useful in scenarios where false positives are costly or undesirable.

Here are some examples to illustrate this:

• Medical Diagnosis: Imagine a zero-shot classifier as a new medical test that can diagnose

diseases it hasn’t seen during training. Precision is crucial here because a false positive (wrongly

diagnosing a healthy person as sick) can lead to unnecessary stress, treatments, and costs.

• Content Moderation: A social media platform uses a zero-shot classifier to flag harmful

content. High precision is important because incorrectly flagging benign content as harmful

(false positive) can lead to censorship and user dissatisfaction.

• Financial Fraud Detection: Think of the classifier as a bank’s fraud detection system. High

precision means it accurately flags fraudulent transactions without bothering customers with

false alarms (legitimate transactions flagged as fraud), ensuring customer trust.

• Email Spam Filtering: A zero-shot classifier is used to filter spam emails. Precision is key

because users don’t want important emails mistakenly classified as spam (false positives).

• Product Recommendation Systems: Consider a zero-shot classifier as a personal shopping

assistant that recommends products. High precision ensures that it recommends only relevant

products.

• Automated Customer Support: In a scenario where a zero-shot classifier is used to route

customer queries to appropriate departments, high precision ensures that queries are correctly

categorized.

• Safety-Critical Systems: Imagine a zero-shot classifier in an autonomous vehicle, identifying

objects on the road. High precision is vital to avoid false positives (e.g., mistaking a paper bag

for a rock), which could lead to unnecessary or dangerous maneuvers.

In each of the above examples, the cost of a false positive is high, making precision a critical measure

of the classifier’s performance.

Fine-Tuning and Best Practices

Few-Shot Learning

Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 and GPT-4 have been pre-trained using an enormous

amount of data from the open web, which consists of billions of words. This extensive training has

transformed them into incredibly powerful tools capable of rapidly learning new tasks from just

a few examples. This concept is known as “few-shot learning,” and it represents a groundbreaking

advancement in the field of AI.

Undoubtedly, there are numerous other potent open-source few-shot learning projects available⁵⁶.

To implement these few-shot learning projects, there are several robust Python libraries at your

disposal:

• Pytorch – Torchmeta⁵⁷: This is a collection of extensions and data-loaders for few-shot learning

and meta-learning in PyTorch⁵⁸.

• Few Shot⁵⁹: This repository contains clean, legible, and verified code for reproducing few-shot

learning research.

• FewRel⁶⁰: This is a large-scale few-shot relation extraction dataset, which includes more than

a hundred relations and tens of thousands of annotated instances across various domains.

• Few-Shot Object Detection (FsDet)⁶¹: This contains the official few-shot object detection

implementation of Simple Few-Shot Object Detection⁶².

• Meta Transfer Learning⁶³: This is a framework designed to tackle the challenging few-shot

learning setting. The goal of this project is to leverage multiple similar low-sample tasks to

learn how to modify a base learner for a new task with only a few labeled samples available.

• Prototypical Networks on the Omniglot Dataset⁶⁴: This is an implementation of “Prototypical

Networks for Few-shot Learning” on a notebook in Pytorch.

• And more

The “few-shot learning” capability enables GPT models to quickly “understand” the instructions

given to them, even with minimal data. In simpler terms, Large Language Models like GPT-3, GPT-

4, and others can be programmed to accomplish tasks with only a few examples as input. This

breakthrough paves the way for limitless possibilities in AI-driven applications and other related

fields.

Fine-Tuning and Best Practices 173

Enhancing Few-Shot Learning

The principle of fine-tuning is a method of enhancing few-shot learning by training on a

significantly larger number of examples than can be accommodated in the prompt. This strategy

can be employed to attain superior outcomes across a broad spectrum of tasks:

• Augmenting the quantity of examples utilized

• Enhancing the precision of the results

• Expanding the array of tasks that can be accomplished

Once a model has been refined and enhanced, it’s no longer necessary to supply examples when you

submit a request.

This approach is cost-effective and accelerates requests: You only need to provide examples when

you aim to enhance the model, after which you can operate it using prompts alone, without examples.

Bear in mind, the lengthier your prompt, the more OpenAI will bill you.

Fine-tuning is applicable for the following models:

• GPT-3.5-Turbo-1106

• GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613

• Babbage-002

• Davinci-002

• GPT-4-0613

This list is subject to alterations. In the future, OpenAI plans to introduce more models and retire

some. Among these models, GPT-3.5-Turbo-1106 is the most potent, and OpenAI advocates its use

for fine-tuning. Some models, such as GPT-4-0613, are still in the experimental phase.

Token Limit

The maximum number of tokens per message depends on the model you choose. For GPT-3.5-Turbo,

the maximum number of tokens per message is 16,385. For GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613, the maximum

number of tokens per message is 4,096. If a message exceeds the maximum number of tokens, it

will be truncated to fit within the limit, which may result in a loss of information. Make sure that

the entire dataset does not exceed the maximum number of tokens.

Dataset Size

The size of the dataset is a crucial factor in fine-tuning. A minimum of 10 examples is required, but

OpenAI recommends using at least 50 to 100 examples with GPT-3.5-Turbo. Generally, the more

examples you provide, the better the results will be.

The maximum file upload size is 1 GB. However, OpenAI does not recommend fine-tuning with that

amount of data as you are unlikely to need such a large amount to see improvements. Additionally,

the larger the file, the longer it will take to upload, process, and train.

text:
Fine-Tuning and Best Practices 192

Testing and Improving Training (Hyperparameters)

After the training phase, you can evaluate the model’s performance through a regular chat session. If

the results don’t meet your expectations, you can retrain the model using different hyperparameters.

Initially, OpenAI suggests fine-tuning without specifying any hyperparameters, allowing the model

to choose default values based on the size of the dataset. If the results still don’t meet your

expectations, you can then adjust the number of epochs, learning rate multiplier, and batch size.

Epochs

An epoch refers to the number of times the learning algorithm will process the entire training dataset.

During each epoch, the model is exposed to all examples in the training dataset once. This means

that if your dataset contains 500 examples, one epoch would involve the model processing all 500

examples. As it processes each example, the model makes predictions and adjusts its internal learning

parameters based on the discrepancy between its predictions and the actual data.

In some instances, a single pass through the dataset (an epoch) may not provide sufficient learning

for the model. Therefore, it may be necessary to run multiple epochs. Each epoch provides another

opportunity for the model to learn from the data, improve its predictions, and further reduce its loss.

Adjusting the number of epochs can help improve results, but excessively increasing it may lead to

overfitting.

ℹ Overfitting happens when a learning model performs exceptionally well on its training

data but fails to generalize effectively to unseen or test data. The model absorbs all the

detail and noise in the training data to such an extent that it negatively impacts the

model’s performance on new data.

The process of adjusting the number of epochs (and any hyperparameter tuning in general) is

iterative. You should start with a small number of epochs and gradually increase it until you achieve

the desired results. If you notice that the model is overfitting and/or lacking diversity, you should

reduce the number of epochs slightly, test, and repeat as necessary.

Here’s how you can adjust the number of epochs. In this example, we’re using 10 epochs:

1 client.fine_tuning.jobs.create(

2 training_file=file_id,

3 model=model,

4 hyperparameters={

5 "n_epochs": 10

6 }

7 )

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text:
Fine-Tuning and Best Practices 193

Learning Rate Multiplier

This factor modifies the base learning rate used during the training process. It determines the size of

the steps that the model takes during the optimization process and controls how much the model’s

weights are updated during training.

Think of training a machine learning model as teaching a person how to navigate a maze. The

learning rate is similar to the size of the steps the person takes while exploring the maze.

When navigating the maze, the person can take large or small steps. A larger step (higher learning

rate) means covering more ground quickly, but there’s a risk of overshooting and missing the correct

path. Conversely, a smaller step (lower learning rate) means moving cautiously: no detail is missed,

but it takes longer to find the exit.

Adjusting the learning rate for a model when fine-tuning is akin to adjusting the step size for a

person learning to navigate a maze. If the model doesn’t seem to be converging (i.e., not improving

its performance on the training data), increasing the learning rate multiplier might help. However,

this should be done cautiously to avoid the risks associated with a too high learning rate.

Here’s how you can adjust the learning rate multiplier. In this example, we’re using 1.5:

1 client.fine_tuning.jobs.create(

2 training_file=file_id,

3 model=model,

4 hyperparameters={

5 "learning_rate_multiplier": 1.5

6 }

7 )

ℹ Generally, a machine learning model reaches convergence when its loss function stops

decreasing. The loss function measures how accurately the model predicts the target

variable. The lower the loss, the better the model predicts the target variable given the

input data. The loss function is calculated during the training process, and the model’s

weights are updated to minimize the loss. When the loss stops decreasing, the model has

reached convergence.

Batch Size

In simple terms, the batch size is the number of examples that the model processes at once. This

hyperparameter can be adjusted to enhance the model’s performance.

Consider the batch size as analogous to loading a delivery truck. Each item in the truck represents a

training example, and the batch size is the number of items you load onto the truck at once. Just as

the truck has a limited capacity, the algorithm processes a specific number of examples per iteration.

Larger batch sizes can reduce the total number of iterations needed to process the entire dataset,

as more examples are processed per iteration. However, this doesn’t always result in faster overall

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development

Fine-Tuning and Best Practices 194

training times. Larger batches can slow down the convergence rate because the model updates its

weights less frequently. On the other hand, smaller batch sizes lead to more frequent updates but

require more iterations to process the entire dataset, which could potentially extend training times.

Here’s how to change the batch size (in this example, we’re using 32):

1 client.fine_tuning.jobs.create(

2 training_file=file_id,

3 model=model,

4 hyperparameters={

5 "batch_size": 32

6 }

7 )

Consider Estimated Costs

Before fine-tuning a model, it’s important to consider the costs associated with training, input usage,

and output usage. If you are testing with a small dataset, the costs may be negligible. However, as

the dataset grows and the model is used more frequently, the costs can add up. Let’s see how the

costs compare for different models and usage types.

Training Cost: GPT-3.5-Turbo is the most expensive model to train. In contrast, Babbage-002 is the

least expensive for training, costing $0.0004 per 1K tokens.

ℹ The training cost is associated with fine-tuning the model on your specific dataset. When

you train (or fine-tune) a model, you’re essentially updating its parameters to better suit

your data and use case. The cost is calculated based on the number of tokens in your

training dataset and is charged per 1,000 tokens. This is a one-time cost incurred during

the training process.

Input Cost: Davinci-002 is the most expensive model for input, costing $0.0120 per 1K tokens.

Babbage-002 is the least expensive for input, costing $0.0016 per 1K tokens.

ℹ Input usage refers to the cost of tokens that you send to the model as input during regular

use after training (i.e., when you make requests to the model for predictions or responses).

For example, if you send a prompt to the model to generate text, the number of tokens in

your prompt counts as input usage.

Output Cost: Davinci-002 is the most expensive model for output, costing $0.0120 per 1K tokens.

Babbage-002 is the least expensive for output, costing $0.0016 per 1K tokens.

ℹ The cost of output is associated with the number of tokens generated by the model in

response to your inputs. In other words, each token in the output counts towards the

billing.

The table below summarizes the costs:

In the long term, the cost of fine-tuning becomes negligible compared to the recurring costs of input

and output usage, as it’s a one-time expense. Therefore, using GPT-3.5-Turbo for fine-tuning is a

cost-effective choice that balances between cost and performance over time.

Dataset Quality

The quality of your dataset is a crucial factor in fine-tuning. For optimal results, your dataset should

be relevant to the task you aim to accomplish. For instance, if you’re creating a chatbot for a specific

domain, you should start by clearly defining the following elements:

• The domain: Identify the specific field or area your chatbot will specialize in.

• The problem you want to solve: Identify the specific issues or queries your chatbot is designed

to handle.

• The target audience: Define who your chatbot is intended for.

• The language: Specify the language or languages your chatbot will support.

• The tone: Decide on the tone your chatbot’s responses should have. For example, a healthcare

chatbot might use a professional, informative tone, while a gaming website’s chatbot might be

more casual and playful.

Moreover, it’s important to ensure your data is clean, relevant, and well-structured. Avoid biases as

they can lead to suboptimal results.

Combining Fine-Tuning with Other Techniques

Fine-tuning becomes more effective when combined with other techniques such as prompt engi-

neering, information retrieval, and function calling.

Prompt Engineering is the process of designing prompts to steer the model towards generating

the desired output. For example, if you’re developing a customer service chatbot, instead of using a

generic prompt like “Respond to the customer,” you could employ a more specific prompt like “As

a friendly and helpful customer service assistant, respond to the customer’s inquiry about return

policies.”

The Information Retrieval technique involves integrating the model with a system that retrieves

information from a database or the internet. For instance, in a legal advice chatbot, when a user poses

a specific legal question, the model could be programmed to fetch relevant legal information from a

pre-existing database or trusted legal websites before formulating a response. A popular technique

for this is known as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text:
Fine-Tuning and Best Practices 196

ℹ RAG is an advanced AI language processing method that merges retrieval and generation

techniques. It enhances the ability of AI models to produce accurate and contextually

relevant responses by leveraging external information sources. The method comprises

two main stages: retrieval and generation. In the retrieval stage, RAG employs a retrieval

mechanism to collect pertinent information from a vast external knowledge base. This

data could originate from articles, web pages, or any structured or unstructured text.

The retrieval can be based on keyword matching, semantic search, or other sophisticated

methods to find relevant information for the generation process. The generation stage

then utilizes the information retrieved earlier to generate a response.

Function Calling involves integrating external functions into the model’s responses. For instance, in

a travel recommendation chatbot, when a user requests weather information for a specific location,

the chatbot could invoke an external weather API to obtain current weather data and incorporate

this information into its response.

Experiment and Learn

Fine-tuning is a process of continuous learning. Each fine-tuning job is an opportunity to enhance

your understanding and refine your approach. You may need to adjust and experiment with different

hyperparameters, prompts, dataset sizes, and sometimes even the dataset itself to achieve better

results.

Use a Validation Set

The goal of fine-tuning is to adapt a pre-trained model to perform effectively on a specific task. A

validation set is used to ensure that the model is learning as expected. However, it’s important to

note that the validation set should be a distinct subset of the data, separate from the training data,

not a subset of the training data. This validation set is used to evaluate the model’s performance

during the training process. Its main roles include tuning the model’s hyperparameters and helping

to prevent overfitting by providing feedback on how the model performs on data it hasn’t seen

during training.

Advanced Fine Tuning: Mental Health

Coach

In this chapter, we aim to dive deep into the process of fine-tuning a language model with the end

goal of creating a sophisticated mental health coach chatbot. This chatbot will be equipped with

the capability to provide professionally-backed advice and guidance to users on a broad spectrum

of mental health topics. This includes, but is not limited to, areas such as depression, anxiety, stress

management, and many more pertinent issues that individuals may face in their daily lives.

To achieve this, we will walk you through a systematic step-by-step guide, starting with how

to effectively prepare the data set required for this task. This involves collecting, cleaning, and

processing the data in a way that optimizes the performance of our model. Following this, we

will dive into the actual fine-tuning of the language model, breaking down complex concepts and

methods into easy-to-understand steps.

Toward the end, we will see the practical aspect of using the model in real-world applications.

This includes understanding its potential limitations, identifying the challenges one might face in a

practical scenario, and providing actionable solutions to overcome them.

Dataset Used in the Example

The dataset, initially downloaded from huggingface.co⁶⁸, is a collection of questions and answers

(in English) sourced from two online counseling and therapy platforms. The questions cover a wide

range of mental health topics, and the answers are provided by qualified psychologists. The dataset

is intended to be used for fine-tuning language models to improve their ability to provide mental

health advice.

The strength of the dataset is that it contains real-world conversations between users and mental

health professionals. This makes it a valuable resource for fine-tuning language models to provide

better mental health advice.

Using the Model in Real-World Applications and

Challenges

You can integrate the model into real-world applications. For instance, it can be used to provide

mental health advice in a chatbot for web or mobile applications, or in a smart home assistant

application. The possibilities are endless.

However, it’s crucial to consider the ethical implications when using the model in real-world

applications. For instance, ensure the model is used responsibly and doesn’t provide harmful advice.

Also, it’s important to use the model in a way that respects the privacy and confidentiality of the

users.

Despite its usefulness, the model isn’t perfect and can provide inaccurate advice. From a functional

perspective, a user might face challenges as the model might not be able to handle a full conversation.

For instance, it might struggle with conversations requiring multiple turns or additional information

from the user. This is because the model is designed to provide a single response to a single input.

The following example illustrates the model’s limitations in handling interactive conversations:

text:
Context & Memory: Making AI More

Real

The Problem: No Memory

GPT is a generative text model, meaning it produces new text by predicting what comes next based

on the user’s input. The model was trained on a large corpus of text, including books, articles, and

websites, and it used this data to learn patterns and relationships between words and phrases.

By default, the model has no memory when you initiate a conversation with it. This means each

input is treated independently, without any context or information carried over from the previous

user prompts. While this may not be ideal for human-friendly interactions, it allows the model to

generate more diverse and less repetitive text.

In some cases, carrying over context is useful and necessary. Techniques like fine-tuning on a specific

topic can improve the quality of outputs, but they are not always efficient, as the conversation can

switch to a different topic at any time.

Let’s experiment with different approaches.

No Context = Chaos of Randomness and Confusion

Let’s start by building a simple chatbot. Initially, we are going to initiate a discussion as our goal is

to compare the outputs of the model now and later when we carry over the context.

The Problem with Carrying Over History

With long discussions, the user prompt will be longer since it will always be added to the history

until it reaches the maximum number of tokens allowed by the OpenAI API. This depends on the

model you are using, but in all cases, there is a limit.

The second problem here is the cost. You are charged by tokens, so the more tokens you add to the

history, the more you will be charged since history is included in the prompt and sent to the API.

One solution to this problem is to only store the most recent prompts and answers. This is what we

are going to see in the next section.

Last In First Out (LIFO) Memory

I’m not sure if this approach has a technical name, but I call it “last in first out” because the idea

behind it is simple:

• Users always initiate discussions with a context.

• The context evolves and so does the discussion.

• Users will most likely include the context in the latest 2 to 5 prompts.

Based on this, we could assume that a better approach is to only store the most recent prompts.

Here’s how it works in a nutshell:

• The history is stored in a file.

• When the user enters a prompt, the program reads the last N prompts from the history and

sends them to the API with the user’s prompt.

• The program then saves the user’s prompt and the response to the history file.

• The history file is updated with the latest prompts and responses.

• The program reads the last N prompts from the history and sends them to the API with the

user’s prompt, and so on.

Context & Memory: Making AI More Real 223

The Problem with Last in First out Memory

The approach I’ve termed “Last In, First Out Memory” may falter when a discussion becomes highly

complex, requiring the user to switch between different contexts. In such instances, the approach

may fail to provide the necessary context as it only retains the most recent prompts. This could lead

to user confusion and frustration, which is not conducive to user-friendly interactions.

For instance, if N equals x, where x is a relatively small number, the model will only consider the

last x prompts and responses. This means that if the discussion extends beyond x prompts, the model

will not be able to provide the necessary context. Conversely, if N equals y, where y is a relatively

large number, the model will consider a substantial number of prompts and responses, which could

be resource-intensive.

In the next section, we will examine a more sophisticated approach that addresses the limitations of

the Last In, First Out Memory.

Selective Context

The solution suggested in this part will work as follows:

• An initial prompt is saved to a text file.

• The user enters a prompt that depends on a context.

• The program creates embeddings for all interactions in the file.

• The program calculates the cosine similarity between the user’s prompt, its context, and the

previous interactions.

• The program sorts the file by the cosine similarity.

• The best n interactions are read from the file and sent with the prompt to the user.

We are using a text file here to simplify things, but as previously stated, you can use any data store.

We are going to use an embedding function to create embeddings for the user’s prompt and all

interactions in the file, as well as a function to calculate the cosine similarity between the user’s

prompt and all interactions in the file. The selection occurs at the level of loading the history from

the file.

This is what we need to use as a starting point:

Using Vector Database with OpenAI

Introduction

In the previous examples, we attempted to make AI more aware of the dialogue context. However,

we utilized text files for context storage, which is not the most efficient method. Therefore, we will

use a database for context storage, specifically a vector database.

There are numerous popular vector databases, including Faiss, Annoy, Milvus, Weaviate, etc. In this

example, we will use Weaviate. Before we begin, let’s understand what a vector database is.

What is a Vector Database?

A vector database is a type of database designed for storing, indexing, and querying vectors

(arrays of numbers representing data in a high-dimensional space). Vectors often come from the

transformation of unstructured data, such as images, text, or sound, into a numerical format that

can be processed and analyzed by machine learning models, particularly those involving similarity

search and nearest neighbor algorithms.

Vector databases are excellent for some AI applications, such as recommendation systems, search

engines, and natural language processing where the goal is to find items most similar to a query

item based on their vector representations.

Imagine you’re in a vast library full of books, but instead of traditional genres or titles, every book is

represented by a unique pattern of stars in the sky. Each pattern (or “vector”) represents the essence

of a book - its theme, style, and content - translated into a language of stars that only the library’s

magical telescope (the “vector database”) can understand and interpret.

Think of each book in the library as a piece of data (a document, an image, or even a sound clip)

in the real world. Converting these books into star patterns is similar to transforming unstructured

data into vectors using ML models such as GPT models. Each vector is a numerical representation

that captures the essence of the data in a high-dimensional space.

This telescope is special - think of it as the vector database - it can quickly scan the night sky (search

through the database) and find patterns similar to the one you’re interested in. When you’re curious

about a topic, you describe it to the telescope, and it translates your description into a star pattern.

Let’s say you’re fascinated by stories about dragons. You tell this to the telescope. It creates a star

pattern representing “dragon stories” and scans the sky, looking for similar patterns. The patterns

closest to your “dragon story” pattern are the books (data) most relevant to your interest. This process

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text:
Using Vector Database with OpenAI 234

is akin to performing a similarity search in a vector database, where the system finds data points

(vectors) closest to your query vector.

The goal of this metaphor is to help you visualize the whole concept from embedding data into

vectors to querying a vector database.

The metaphor “interpreted” by DALL-E

Here are some real-world examples of how applications use vector databases:

• Recommendation Systems: A vector database can store user preferences and item features

subject: Technical / AI / OpenAI / Python Development
text:
Using Vector Database with OpenAI 235

as vectors. When a user searches for a product, the system finds the most similar items to

recommend.

• Voice Recognition: When you speak to a voice assistant, your speech is converted into a vector.

The assistant searches for the best match to understand your commands.

• Image Search: You upload a picture of a car, and the vector database helps you find other

images of cars. The system translates the visual characteristics into vectors and compares them

to other images that are also represented as vectors in the same database.

Vector databases are fast and efficient at finding the most similar vectors to a query vector.

They use specialized indexing structures to efficiently store and query high-dimensional vectors.

These structures, such as k-d trees⁷¹, HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) graphs⁷², or

quantization-based indexes, help in reducing the dimensionality and speeding up the search for

the nearest neighbors.

Example 1: Using Weaviate to Make Our Model More

Context-Aware

In this example, we will create two Docker containers: one for Weaviate and another for our AI

model. We will use Docker Compose to manage these containers.

We are building an API with a single endpoint to interact with the user’s request (question). The

API will send the question to Weaviate and retrieve the most similar context from Weaviate. Then,

it will send the context to the OpenAI API to get the answer. The answer will be sent back to the

user, and it will also be stored in Weaviate for future use. The user can see the output of the API in

the browser, the terminal, or any other client like Postman.

Example 2: Using Weaviate and OpenAI in Semantic

Search

In this example, we are going to use Weaviate and OpenAI to build a semantic search engine.

Weaviate will store the data as well as the vectors representing the data. OpenAI will be used to

perform a semantic search through the vectors.

We are going to use a CSV dataset containing articles from Simple English Wikipedia. The dataset

is hosted by OpenAI⁷⁴. Alternatively, you can download the dataset from this GitHub repository

eon01/Openai_GPT_for_Python_Developers_Files⁷⁵.

The CSV file contains the following columns:

• “id”: the unique identifier of the data entry.

• “url”: the URL of the Wikipedia page.

• “title”: the title of the article.

• “text”: the content of the article.

• “content_vector”: the vector representation of the content.

Note that the vectorization was done using the OpenAI text-embedding-ada-002 model.

The function weaviate_semantic_search() is designed to perform a semantic search within a

Weaviate database using a specified query.

At its core, the function leverages Weaviate’s vector search capabilities to find entries that are

semantically related to the input query. By constructing a nearText dictionary with the query

encapsulated in a list under the concepts key, it directs Weaviate to evaluate the semantic closeness

of the database entries to the provided query concepts.

The function requests the title and content properties of the matching entries, along with an

additional piece of information labeled distance. This distance is crucial as it quantifies how close

each returned entry is to the query in the vector space, with a lower distance indicating higher

similarity.

The use of a limit set to 2 constrains the search to return only the top two most relevant entries.

The choice of including _additional {distance} in the properties list is particularly interesting, as

it provides insight into the semantic search process by revealing the raw distances calculated during

the search. This offers a transparent view into why certain entries were considered more relevant

than others.

Example 3: Using Weaviate and OpenAI for Generative

Search

Generative search is a type of search that generates new content based on the user’s query.

When we search for a term in a search engine, we typically receive a list of results relevant to the

query. However, in some instances, we may want to generate new content based on the query. For

instance, if we search for “how to make a cake”, we might want to receive a cake recipe instead of a

list of websites containing the term “how to make a cake”.

The same principle applies to our example. For instance, when we search the word “cat”, we can

generate a new article about cats based on the query “cat” and the returned context. Weaviate will

return the most relevant articles based on the query and send a message to OpenAI to generate a

new article based on the context.

We will maintain the same Dockerfiles and the application .env file, as well as the “docker-

compose.yml” file and “requirements.txt” file. Two things will change in this example:

• The Weaviate container’s “.env” file.

• The “app.py” file.

6 DEFAULT_VECTORIZER_MODULE=text2vec-openai

7 ENABLE_MODULES=text2vec-openai,generative-openai

8 CLUSTER_HOSTNAME=node1

enables the generative module in Weaviate.

Speech Recognition and Translation

Using Whisper

What is Whisper?

Whisper is an ASR system (Automatic Speech Recognition) and a general-purpose speech recog-

nition model trained by OpenAI on 680,000 hours of multilingual and multitask supervised data

collected from the web.

OpenAI reports that using a large, varied dataset has increased robustness to accents, background

noise, and technical terminology. Furthermore, it has enabled transcription in multiple languages,

as well as translation from those languages into English.

These are the supported languages:

Afrikaans, Arabic, Armenian, Azerbaijani, Belarusian, Bosnian, Bulgarian, Catalan, Chinese, Croat-

ian, Czech, Danish, Dutch, English, Estonian, Finnish, French, Galician, German, Greek, Hebrew,

Hindi, Hungarian, Icelandic, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Kannada, Kazakh, Korean, Latvian,

Lithuanian, Macedonian, Malay, Marathi, Maori, Nepali, Norwegian, Persian, Polish, Portuguese,

Romanian, Russian, Serbian, Slovak, Slovenian, Spanish, Swahili, Swedish, Tagalog, Tamil, Thai,

Turkish, Ukrainian, Urdu, Vietnamese, and Welsh.

The model and inference code were open-sourced by OpenAI and can be found on GitHub.

There are five model sizes, four of which have English-only versions. Each model offers a tradeoff

between speed and accuracy. The names of the models, along with their approximate memory

requirements and relative speeds, are listed below.

base 74 M base.en base ∼1 GB ∼16x

large 1550 M N/A large ∼10 GB 1x

The performance of Whisper varies greatly depending on the language, the size of the model, the

quality of the audio, and the model’s version.

How to Get Started?

You’ll need to have Python ≥ 3.8 installed. Activate your development environment:

1 mkvirtualenv -p python3.9 whisper-learning

Then, install Whisper using the following command:

1 pip install -U openai-whisper==20231117

You also need to install “ffmpeg” on your system:

On Ubuntu or Debian:

1 apt update

2 apt install ffmpeg

on Arch Linux:

1 pacman -S ffmpeg

on MacOS using Homebrew:

1 brew install ffmpeg

on Windows using Chocolatey:

1 choco install ffmpeg

on Windows using Scoop:

1 scoop install ffmpeg

Install “setuptools-rust”:

1 pip install setuptools-rust==1.8.1

Let’s download an audio file containing a speech for testing. You can find many files on Wikipedia⁷⁸.

⁷⁸https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Audio_files_of_speeches

Transcribe and Translate

The model can also translate speech. The audio is transcribed into text and then translated into

English.

For example, let’s consider this Russian speech:

1 wget \

2 https://upload.wikimedia.org/\

3 wikipedia/commons/1/1a/\

4 Lenin_-_What_Is_Soviet_Power.ogg \

5 -O src/whisper/audio/Lenin.ogg

Then execute:

1 whisper \

2 src/whisper/audio/Lenin.ogg \

3 --language Russian \

4 --task translate

You should be able to view the translation line-by-line.

1 [00:00.000 --> 00:02.000] What is Soviet power?

2 [00:02.000 --> 00:06.000] What is the essence of this new power,

3 [00:06.000 --> 00:11.000] which cannot be understood in most countries?

4 [00:11.000 --> 00:15.000] The essence of it is attracting workers.

5 [00:15.000 --> 00:19.000] In each country, more and more people stand up

6 [00:19.000 --> 00:22.000] to the Prime Minister of the State,

7 [00:22.000 --> 00:25.000] such as other rich or capitalists,

8 [00:25.000 --> 00:29.000] and now for the first time control the state.

There are some parameters you can adjust to enhance both transcription and translation. For

example, we can increase the temperature and the number of candidates when sampling to obtain

different results.

Here is an example:

Using OpenAI Speech to Text API

OpenAI also provides a REST API for Whisper. There are two endpoints you can use:

• One for transcription: You can use it to transcribe audio files into text in multiple languages.

• One for translation: You can use it to translate and transcribe audio files into English.

OpenAI limits the upload size to 25MB, but this may change in the future. Your audio file should be

in one of the following formats: mp3, mp4, mpeg, mpga, m4a, wav, or webm.

Transcription API

Start by activating your virtual environment where you installed the “openai” SDK:

1 workon openaigptforpythondevelopers

We already created the “src/api.py” file in one of the previous chapters. We will use it to authenticate

with the API. Here is the file content:

2 from openai import OpenAI

3

4 with open("src/.env") as env:

5 for line in env:

6 key, value = line.strip().split("=")

7 os.environ[key] = value

8

9 client = OpenAI(

10 api_key=os.environ['API_KEY'],

11 organization=os.environ['ORG_ID']

12 )

The “.env” file should contain the following:

1 API_KEY=sk-...

2 ORG_ID=org-...

Speech Recognition and Translation Using Whisper 284

Improving Whisper Transcription

One of the challenges of using Whisper is that it may not always transcribe the audio accurately.

This is especially true when the audio quality is poor. It may also struggle with uncommon words,

technical terms, and specialized vocabulary.

Next, we will explore some techniques to improve transcription accuracy.

Cleaning the Audio

The first thing you can do to improve transcription accuracy is to clean the audio. This involves

removing any background noise, echoes, and other sounds that may interfere with speech.

You can use a tool like Audacity to clean the audio. Audacity is a free, open-source, cross-platform

audio software that allows you to record and edit audio files. Other options include noisereduce⁷⁹,

librosa⁸⁰, PyDub⁸¹, audiomentations⁸², and many others.

Using the Prompt Parameter

A useful feature that can enhance the accuracy of transcription is the ability to provide a prompt. To

improve transcription accuracy for uncommon words or acronyms using Whisper, you can use the

prompt parameter to pass a dictionary with the correct spellings of specialized terms. This approach

helps Whisper recognize and accurately transcribe difficult or unusual words by providing it with

context or a hint.

Whisper will only process the first 244 tokens of the prompt. The list of specific terms or acronyms

(e.g., product SKUs, technical terms) must be relatively short to fit within this limit.

Let’s see an example of how to use the prompt parameter. Download this audio quote from the Matrix

movie:

Text-to-Speech with OpenAI TTS

Models

OpenAI’s Text-to-Speech (TTS) models, namely TTS-1 and TTS-1-HD, are designed to convert

written text into natural-sounding spoken audio.

The TTS-1 model is specifically optimized for real-time text-to-speech applications, offering a

balance between performance and speed. This makes it ideal for interactive use cases where

immediate vocal feedback is crucial.

On the other hand, the TTS-1-HD variant focuses on delivering higher quality audio output. It is

suitable for use cases where clarity, richness, and overall audio fidelity are paramount. This model

variant is especially beneficial for content creation, audiobooks, and any application where the

quality of the speech synthesis significantly impacts the user experience.

Both models leverage OpenAI’s advanced neural network architectures. They are trained on a

diverse dataset of human speech, enabling them to generate natural-sounding audio that closely

resembles human speech patterns (nuances, intonation, emotion, etc.).

Let’s start by creating a text file where we will write the text we want to convert into speech. We

will then use the OpenAI API to convert the text into speech.

Create a new file called “speech.txt” in the “src/data/tts” directory and write the following text:

1 # Create the directory

2 mkdir -p src/data/tts

3 # Create the text file

4 cat << EOF > src/data/tts/speech.txt

5 Hello, Neo - Welcome to the Matrix.

6 EOF

Using AI Avatar Models

The goal here is to create a talking head that can be used to visualize the conversation and make

it more engaging. There are many tools that can be used to create AI avatars, such as Synthesia⁸³,

Rosebud⁸⁴, and RunwayML⁸⁵. These tools use AI models to generate the facial expressions and lip

movements of the avatar. You can integrate with some of these tools using their APIs, and this can

be done in the Flask app.

Another choice is using Open Source tools like SadTalker⁸⁶ and DeepFaceLab⁸⁷ for deepfake videos.

In our example, we are going to use SadTalker to create the talking head.

What’s Next?

In this chapter, we learned how to create an autonomous AI-to-AI discussion system using OpenAI’s

models and Weaviate. We also learned how to use AI avatars to visualize the conversation and

make it more engaging. We used SadTalker to create the talking head, but you can use other tools

like Synthesia, Rosebud, or RunwayML. You can also use Open Source tools like SadTalker and

DeepFaceLab for deepfake videos.

As a next step, to solidify your understanding and skills, you can implement an AutoGPT application

where the user can input a topic, and the application will generate a conversation between more

than 2 AI agents where each agent represents a different viewpoint or expert knowledge on the

topic. These AI agents could simulate a panel discussion, providing diverse insights, arguments,

and perspectives. For instance, in a discussion about climate change, one agent could represent an

environmental scientist, another an economist, and a third could be a policy maker. The conversation

would evolve based on the input topic, with each AI agent contributing based on its assigned role,

leading to a multifaceted exploration of the subject.
